strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why adversarially trained models can generalize well on clean data while exhibiting a large robust generalization gap. The CGRO definition clearly separates the relevant performance criteria.

Combining representation complexity with signal/noise learning dynamics is a useful conceptual approach. The proposed three-stage mechanism offers an interpretable account of how feature learning and memorization might coexist.
The manuscript provides substantial proof detail and complementary empirical illustrations, including model-capacity sweeps, synthetic feature trajectories, and measurements of input-loss flatness.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider a balanced distribution on (e_1,+1) and (-e_1,-1), with radius δ=1/4 and f_clean(x)=x_1+8x_2. This satisfies boundedness, class separation, and existence of a small clean but nonrobust classifier. With N equal to the dimension, both support points appear with frequencies near 1/2 with high probability. Consequently, o(1) robust training error forces zero robust test error, making CGRO impossible. Additional conditions controlling distribution mass and sample size are necessary.

The representation construction has further proof gaps. Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes; it does not imply disjoint perturbation balls around all training examples, as asserted after Lemma 4.5. This also invalidates the subsequent algebraic rewriting when same-class balls overlap. Furthermore, Appendix F claims vanishing uniform approximation of the generally discontinuous f_S by continuous ReLU networks. Softening indicators does not establish this claim; transition regions and classification margins require explicit treatment.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish robust training performance under the threat model defining CGRO. Section 5 restricts attacks to the true-signal direction in the signal patch, whereas Definition 3.3 maximizes over the entire perturbation ball. Vanishing loss against the restricted attacks cannot certify small robust training error against unrestricted attacks. The restricted attack can validly lower-bound robust test error, but this does not repair the missing training guarantee.

The training-dynamics proof contains substantive mathematical errors. Lemma 5.11 absorbs the factor (1−λ) into a constant although Assumption 5.7 permits λ=1; at that endpoint, signal growth instead depends on the much smaller residual signal α−δ. Appendix E.12 also treats cubic polynomials of Gaussian noise as sub-Gaussian, which is generally false, and does not adequately account for dependence across neurons sharing the same noise. These steps underpin the phase timing and clean-generalization conclusions.

The synthetic experiment does not satisfy the claimed theoretical regime: it sets δ=α=10, whereas Assumption 5.7 requires δ<α. The permitted attack can therefore erase the entire meaningful signal, leaving label-independent noise. Poor robust generalization is then unavoidable even for an ideal learner, so this experiment cannot validate the claimed optimization mechanism in a robustly learnable setting.

The real-image experiments illustrate accuracy gaps but provide limited evidence for the specific mechanism. Capacity sweeps do not establish exponential representation requirements, and local-flatness measurements do not uniquely identify memorization through local indicators. Missing PGD step counts, step sizes, restart settings, and repeated-run uncertainty also limit reproducibility and confidence in the robustness measurements.

The lower-bound contribution relative to Li et al. (2022) needs clearer justification. Appendix F still constructs a linearly separable hard instance; an existential lower bound over a broader distribution class does not itself strengthen the earlier existential result. Moreover, this worst-case construction is separate from the structured distribution used for the dynamics analysis, so it does not establish that representation complexity causes the analyzed learning behavior.
